title: Why We Get Angry
desc: A message from someone you love, a long day, an empty stomach, and suddenly you're furious. In this calm, sourced deep dive we follow one imagined person, Sam, through one evening and one unsent message, and explore why we get angry: what anger does in the body, what it's for, why hunger, short sleep and heat make it easier, why venting backfires, and the small, research-based steps that actually help. Settle in, it ends with a gentle wind-down.
plan: b01: hook. Sam (an imagined person, say so) on a Thursday evening: skipped lunch, slept about five hours, sits on the bus in a warm, noisy evening; his brother texts 'You forgot again?' and Sam types a sharp reply, thumb over send. 'Tonight, we'll explore' list (what anger is, what it's for, why small things set it off, hunger/sleep/heat, venting myth, what actually helps). End: we'll follow Sam's evening, and come back to that unsent message.
b02: anger is ordinary (F1 Averill): how often, at whom (mostly people we love), 85% felt wronged, what people do afterwards. Why the brother, not a stranger. Sam's message as a typical case.

b03: the body (F2 Cannon 1915): what Sam's body does in seconds, heat in the face, heart, tense hands; fight or flight; that this was built for action, not for texting. Calm explanation, no scary language.
b04: what anger is for (F3 Carver & Harmon-Jones 2009): approach emotion, pushes toward the obstacle; anger as a signal that something matters / a line was crossed; useful and costly sides.
b05: frustration (F4 Dollard 1939, Berkowitz 1989): blocked goals, and Berkowitz's twist that any unpleasant feeling can feed anger; Sam's day of small frustrations stacking up.
b06: the story we tell (F5 Dodge): hostile attribution bias; reading 'You forgot again?' as an attack; how tone vanishes in text; asking 'is there another reading?'.
b07: hunger (F6 Bushman 2014 voodoo dolls, F7 MacCormack & Lindquist 2019 hangry): the pins, the noise blasts, and the key twist that noticing 'I'm hungry' weakens the effect. Sam skipped lunch.
b08: sleep (F8 Krizan & Hisler 2019): two short nights, annoying noise, more anger; sleepiness explains half. Sam's five hours.
b09: heat and surroundings (F9 Larrick 2011 baseball): heat plus a reason to retaliate; the crowded warm bus; small context nudges, not excuses.

b10: culture and rules (F10 Cohen & Nisbett 1996, F11 Kitayama 2015): the hallway insult; and how expressing anger relates to health differently in the US and Japan. Anger is shaped by where we learned it.
b11: myth versus science: venting (F12 Bushman 2002): the punching bag study in detail; rumination keeps anger warm; why 'letting it out' feels good but feeds the flame.
b12: the cost of staying angry (F13 Mostofsky 2014): careful, association, small absolute risk, not medical advice; Seneca (F16) on delay as a bridge; why the two hours after matter.

b13: what actually helps (F14 Lieberman 2007 naming the feeling, F15 Mischkowski 2012 fly on the wall, F16 delay, F17 Aristotle right person/degree/time). Sam names it ('I'm hungry, tired and hurt'), eats, waits, deletes the draft, writes a calmer, honest reply. Anger as information, not an order.

b14: wind-down 1: practical takeaways as a soft list (notice body, name it, check hunger/sleep/heat, ask 'another reading?', wait, step back, then speak); callback to the opening bus ride and the unsent message.
b15: wind-down 2: guided settling, slow breathing, letting the evening's frustrations drift by like the bus windows passing streetlights; no new facts.
b16: wind-down 3: gentle body scan through the places anger lives (jaw, shoulders, hands, chest), softening each; light callbacks to Cannon's 'body ready for action', now allowed to rest.
b17: wind-down 4: kindness toward the angry part of you; Sam's brother replies warmly; the day's small storms become information; quiet reflection.
b18: wind-down 5: last callbacks (Sam asleep, phone dark, the message sent kindly), thank you, @end teasing the next video 'What Your Personality Really Is'.
